title: Kirsch | Assessing Researcher Data Sharing Practices Using Publicly Available Dataset Metadata: A Reproducible Workflow for Institutional Stakeholders | Journal of Librarianship and Scholarly Communication
content: Abstract: Introduction: Scholarly communities are experiencing increased emphasis on research data sharing and reuse. Given the range of available data repositories and variability in the use of persistent identifiers (PIDs) for individuals and institutions, aggregating datasets by researchers at a specific institution is a significant challenge. We developed a reproducible workflow to evaluate 1) data repository use by researchers at our institutions, 2) metrics of reuse, and 3) quality of metadata records. Methods: We used the DataCite REST API to locate metadata records for datasets with creator affiliation names that matched our institutions. We performed substantial cleaning and deduplication before comparing repository use, citations, usage metrics, and metadata completeness. Results: The most common data repositories were Dryad, Harvard Dataverse, figshare, Zenodo, ICPSR, and one institution’s institutional repository. View, download, and citation counts were available from a limited number of repositories, with some discrepancies between different citation reporting methods. title: Wiley research publishing revenue jumps 12pc on OA growth and Emerald acquisition - Research Information
content:
"Wiley has reported 4% growth in its research division for the first quarter of its 2027 financial year, with publishing revenue climbing 12% as strong demand for open access and the addition of Emerald Publishing boosted the business.

Research revenue reached $293 million for the three months ended 31 July 2026, up 4% both on a reported basis and at constant currency.

Research Publishing revenue increased 12% at constant currency, driven by what Wiley described as strong growth in gold open access and AI licensing, alongside a $13 million contribution from Emerald Publishing following completion of the acquisition during the quarter.

The performance helped offset a 30% decline in Research Solutions revenue, which faced a tough comparison with the same period last year because of AI licensing income. Research Solutions generated $4 million in AI licensing revenue during the quarter, compared with $16 million a year earlier."

title: Six UK universities renew unlimited open access deal with JMIR Publications - Research Information
content:
"Six UK universities have renewed an unlimited open access publishing agreement with JMIR Publications through Jisc, extending the arrangement until July 2027.

Newcastle University, the University of Leeds, University of Manchester, University of Nottingham, University of Southampton and University of Warwick have renewed their participation in JMIR Publications’ Flat-Fee Unlimited Open Access Publishing Agreement.

The model replaces individual article processing charges (APCs) with an institutional publishing subscription, allowing eligible researchers at participating universities to publish without paying an APC.

Corresponding authors affiliated with the six institutions can publish across JMIR Publications’ portfolio of more than 30 Gold Open Access journals, covering research across the digital health sector. The renewed agreement runs until 31 July 2027.

JMIR said the subscription model is designed to reduce the administrative and financial barriers associated with individual APC payments, while giving institutions greater predictability over their open access publishing costs."

title: Project MUSE - The Data Rescue Project: A Crowdsourced Effort to Preserve At-Risk US Federal Data
content: Abstract: The US federal government is the world's largest data publisher. Since Trump's second inauguration, these data are threatened because their scope contravenes regime ideology and the offices that maintain these datasets no longer have adequate staff to preserve and provide access to the data. The Data Rescue Project was launched in 2025 as a community response to this crisis. We organized volunteers to work on data rescues, focusing especially on social data to fill an identified gap in other rescue efforts and emphasizing curation of the datasets for long-term data preservation. Through community-building, we became a coordinating body for the data rescue movement, streamlining communication and preventing duplication of effort in the US and internationally. In this article, we use the Data Rescue Project as a case study on building coalitions to push back against the destruction of digital information. Moreover, the US is not unique in its need for these efforts. The need to rapidly capture data from natural disasters, war zones, or unforeseen crises is a component of the digital preservation ecosystem that has been undercovered in the existing literature. title: Altmetrics and Traditional Citation Impact among Top Iranian Researchers: A Comparative Analysis of ResearchGate and Academia
content: Abstract: Objective: The rapid expansion of digital communication has introduced alternative indicators of research visibility and impact, transforming traditional scholarly evaluation. This study investigates the potential of academic social networks for assessing the scholarly impact of Iranian researchers through an altmetrics approach. Method: This study employed a quantitative, cross-sectional design focused on the top 1% of Iranian researchers, as identified by the Islamic World Science Citation Center (ISC). Using a stratified sampling method, a sample of 203 researchers was selected across diverse disciplines. Data were collected between June 22, 2025, and June 4, 2026, by retrieving article-level metrics from Scopus, ResearchGate, and Academia.edu. Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient was applied to examine the relationship between Scopus citation counts and platform-specific engagement indicators (reads and views). content: "Building on our popular “Open Access 101” events, SPARC is pleased to announce a new series, Collections & Open Access: Resourcing Open Scholarship, that will dive deeper into topics at the intersection of library collections and Open Access. This series will examine how collections librarians are navigating major changes, including funder public access requirements and evolving publisher business models, and consider what these changes mean for the future of libraries. The series will explore broader trends in the evolution of collections work, the practical realities of how different libraries are approaching these changes, and what lessons other institutions might draw from their experience. title: Available: OA Switchboard plugin for OJS 3.5 | OA Switchboard
content:
Supporting Diamond journals in increasing the visibility of their open access output among research funders, institutions and consortia.

The integration plugin connecting Open Journal Systems (OJS) with the OA Switchboard is now compatible with OJS 3.5.0.x. Journals running OJS 3.5 can start using the plugin right away.

Once enabled, the plugin automatically sends a set of public article metadata to relevant research funders and institutions via the OA Switchboard when an article is published. The metadata is captured at the point of publication and shared with the institutions affiliated with the article’s authors and the funders supporting the underlying research.

This happens automatically, with no additional manual work required from the editorial team, helping diamond open access journals make their published research more visible to the organisations that fund and support it.

title: Don’t Build Another Repository: Building Research Data Support Without Duplicating Infrastructure
content: "When universities begin thinking seriously about open research data, one solution appears almost immediately: build a repository. It sounds logical. It sounds ambitious. It sounds like progress. But at Wrocław University of Science and Technology, the Library asked a different question: what do researchers need first – another platform or a clearer path? Our answer was not to build new infrastructure. It was to build support. The Library launched a dedicated Open Research Data Section around real moments of need: preparing DMPs, understanding FAIR practice, deciding where data should go, and getting help early enough to matter. Instead of launching a standalone repository, we created a curated institutional pathway through RepOD. This allowed us to invest where local impact was greatest: developing librarians into data steward roles, guiding researchers through decisions, and cooperating with the University Project Department so that support begins at proposal stage, not at the end. This poster tells a simple story: transformation does not always begin with building something new. Sometimes it begins by choosing connection over duplication. content: Abstract: The rise of Diamond Open Access (DOA) represents a major transformation in scholarly communication, redefining traditional systems of knowledge distribution. This study aimed to assess the awareness, perception and knowledge of DOA publishing practices among researchers in Ghana. A cross-sectional study design was used to conveniently collect data from 237 researchers across various institutions in Ghana. Data were collected using structured questionnaires Via Microsoft Forms and analysed using STATA version 17. title: Public Access, Open Access, and the Need for NIH Governance | Health Policy | JAMA Internal Medicine | JAMA Network
content: Abstract:  In July 2025, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Public Access Policy took effect, marking a landmark commitment to free immediate access to taxpayer-funded research. The policy requires that author accepted manuscripts from NIH-funded research be made publicly available in PubMed Central (PMC) immediately on publication, replacing an earlier policy that allowed publishers a 12-month embargo between publication and free public access.1 Several of the largest publishers have responded by requiring NIH-funded authors to pay open access article processing charges (APCs) to deposit the article in PMC. Although the NIH has stated that compliance does not require APC payment,2 it has not publicly defended this position against publisher practices to the contrary. This Viewpoint examines the resulting confusion between public access and open access, the pay-to-comply publisher practices that conflate the two, and the steps that the NIH must take to fill this gap and promote its public access goals.

title: Stop paying predatory publishers of academic journals—A policy proposal to restore scientific integrity and transparency - Rainey - FEBS Letters - Wiley Online Library
content: Abstract:  Scientific publishing is undergoing a systemic breakdown. Thousands of journals now collect article processing charges (APCs)—increasingly paid from public research funds—while providing minimal editorial oversight. This erodes standards, distorts incentives and threatens public trust in science. APC payments to six major publishers exceeded 8 billion dollars between 2019 and 2023, with almost no transparency over how these fees are set or spent. This cannot continue. We propose that public and institutional funds support journals—whether through APCs, subscriptions or bundled agreements—only where they are accredited against a transparent, enforceable quality standard. Implemented in stages and led by funding bodies and learned societies, such accreditation would narrow the space in which predatory journals operate without resorting to blacklists.

title: Does Open Peer Review Correlate With Better Altmetric Attention Performance?An Empirical Analysis Based on Nature Communications | Research Square
content: Abstract: New academic evaluation indicators such as altmetrics have become crucial for measuring the social impact of research. We explore the association between Open Peer Review (OPR) and the altmetric attention performance of academic papers by selecting 35,852 research papers from Nature Communications published between 2016 and 2022. We divided these papers into two groups those adopting OPR and those not. To address sample confounding bias we used twelve confounding variables alongside Propensity Score Matching while multiple matching algorithms and sensitivity analysis were applied to validate the robustness of our results. Our findings show that papers with OPR had significantly higher Altmetric Attention Scores than those without this review method with an Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT) of 5.411 and a 95% confidence interval of [1.34,9.48]. This study confirms OPR is significantly and positively correlated with expanded dissemination scope and greater influence of academic outputs across social media news coverage and the public domain. title: Advancing open research information: exploring the persistence of proprietary bibliographic databases
content: Abstract: Purpose – “Research information”, which informs how research is searched,conducted, monitored, and evaluated, is usually made available in proprietary databases in ways which often restrict its use. Recently, there has been a movement towards opening research information through the creation of systems such asOpenAlex, but their adoption remains inconsistent. title: Cost of Article Processing Charges to Adhere to National Institutes of Health Public Access Policy | Academic Medicine | JAMA Internal Medicine | JAMA Network
content: Abstract:  In July 2025, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) updated its Public Access Policy, requiring that manuscripts from NIH-funded studies be made publicly available immediately after publication. Publisher-enforced delays on public access (embargoes) are no longer allowed for NIH-funded research.1 In principle, investigators can comply with the policy at no cost by depositing their manuscript in PubMed Central. In practice, many publishers still enforce delays on public access for these manuscripts unless authors pay an article processing charge (APC), typically thousands of dollars.2

title: Improving annotation, access, and comparison of nutritional composition data for underutilized crops | Database | Oxford Academic
content: Abstract: Open and interoperable data infrastructures are essential to advancing food and nutritional security research, yet few data management systems are specifically designed for crop nutritional datasets that support seamless querying, visualization, and comparison. Existing data sources are often syntactically and semantically heterogeneous, creating substantial barriers to interoperability and data reuse, and ultimately limiting the translation of research into sustainable agricultural innovation. To address this gap, we developed an ontology-based data access and integration (OBDI) framework that harmonizes publicly available, heterogeneous plant nutritional datasets within a unified semantic structure. By annotating datasets using established plant science ontologies, we enhanced their Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reusability by providing a scalable mechanism for virtual data integration via a knowledge graph enriched with domain semantics. Our workflow enables consistent comparison and computational reasoning across crop nutritional composition data, supporting both machine and human interpretation. title: SPARC Financial Landscape Analysis 2026: Education Publishers | Zenodo
content: Abstract:  This report examines the financial performance of the three largest US higher education course materials publishers—Pearson, McGraw Hill, and Cengage—covering the period from October 2024 to March 2026. Commissioned by SPARC and authored by market analyst Claudio Aspesi, it finds that despite improving operating results across all three companies, investors have responded with skepticism about the sector's exposure to AI, from direct substitution of course content to rising dependence on external AI infrastructure providers, along with investment levels that remain modest relative to management's stated ambitions.

title: Asking the harder question: what happens when article growth outruns the agreement? - Council of Australasian University Librarians
content:
"Article growth has moved from a background trend to a live procurement problem. Publication volumes across CAUL’s portfolios are now exceeding the growth rates that capped agreements were budgeted against, in several cases outpacing 2026 estimates set only months earlier. When volume assumptions break down mid-term, pricing models built on last year’s data are out of date before the next agreement is signed.

The structural difficulty is that the decisions driving volume sit almost entirely on one side of the table. Publishers set title launches, cascading and transfer pathways, and acceptance policy. Libraries absorb the cost consequences without a lever over any of them. Meanwhile, faster submission growth is straining editorial and research integrity processes, with rising desk-rejection rates and AI-assisted submissions widely acknowledged as new pressure points. Global output is on pace to pass six million articles in 2026, up from roughly 5.5 million the year before."

title: HathiTrust Receives Grant to Deliver AI-Enabled Access to Digital Books – HathiTrust Digital Library
content:
"Researchers, students, and the broader public will have new paths into the HathiTrust collection thanks to a Mellon Foundation award to develop responsible, equitable, and transparent services that leverage AI for the public good and scholarly discovery. Two respected collaborators will join HathiTrust in this effort: Northeastern University Library, which brings deep expertise in digital scholarship, and Authors Alliance, a nonprofit that supports authors who want their work to benefit the public. With a firm commitment to lawful, noncommercial, public-interest uses, this project will make HathiTrust’s 19 million digitized volumes more useful and accessible to the academic community and the public.

Transparent Books: AI Infrastructure for Discovery and the Public Interest responds to the growing need for shared, trusted, academy-led infrastructure enabling sophisticated discovery and research of digitized collections. The project aims to connect readers to relevant titles more efficiently, thereby enhancing their reach and impact, and will consider a range of interests, including publishers, authors, scholars, and members of the public."

title: Archiving Democracy: How the U.S. End of Term Web Archive Preserves Government History | Internet Archive Blogs
content:
"Beginning in January 2025, we witnessed an unprecedented removal of material from U.S. federal websites — documents related to education, health, science, and more, gone from public view almost overnight. Dozens of articles appeared on this topic, including this one from IEEE Spectrum, published in February 2025, shortly after the beginning of the new presidential term. The author, Gwendolyn Rak, like many other doing research in this area, noted that not only did individual web pages change or vanish almost overnight, but that the web presence of entire agencies such as the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) disappeared from view. Moments like this are exactly why libraries have collaborated to build the End of Term Web Archive.

The Internet Archive has participated in the End of Term (EOT) Archive since 2004, working alongside partner institutions to capture US government websites at every presidential transition. Over time the scope has grown, but the purpose remains the same: to preserve government information and civic memory at critical moments of democratic change."

title: Parkinson’s Research Funders Lead the Way with Progressive Open Access and Open Science Policies - SPARC
content:
"To accelerate the understanding of Parkinson’s disease, improve treatment, and, ultimately, find a cure, two prominent funders in the field have recently expanded their requirements for grantees to share their findings.

The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research (MJFF) and Aligning Science Across Parkinson’s (ASAP) use open science policies to ensure information at all stages in the research process are accessible to all. The two organizations work closely together to advance Parkinson’s research. MJFF serves as an implementation partner for ASAP-supported programs and helps translate shared priorities around collaboration, resource generation and open data sharing into practice.

Both organizations are members of the Open Research Funders Group where they are held up as models for their policies and dedicating resources to support scientists data sharing, says Michele Avissar-Whiting, who serves as an ORFG coordinating committee member and is director of open science strategy at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute."

title: Guest post: The uncomfortable truth an explosion of papers reveals about authors’ access to data – Retraction Watch
content:
"The involvement of independent academic researchers in examining data and conducting analyses is central to producing trustworthy research. Because of this, many journals require authors to sign a statement acknowledging they “had full access to all the data in the study,” and take “responsibility for the integrity of the data and the accuracy of the data analysis.” Indeed, the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) recommendations for authorship note that authors should be “accountable for all aspects of the work.” 

A rapidly increasing number of published articles rely on analyses produced via the TriNetX platform. However, TriNetX users don’t get full access to the information in the platform, muddying the truthfulness of any analyses of the data and compromising the integrity statements offered by authors and accepted by journals."

title: What is the future of the Biodiversity Heritage Library? – News Bureau
content: "The Biodiversity Heritage Library is the world’s largest open access digital library dedicated to biodiversity literature. The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Library has been a member of the BHL’s global consortium since 2014 and a contributor of materials since 2007. Kelli Trei, the biosciences librarian and a professor in the University Library and the vice chair for the biodiversity library’s executive committee, was selected as the BHL transition director in 2025 after the Smithsonian Institution, which had hosted the library’s operations since its founding in 2006, announced it would cease that role. She oversaw the relocation of the library’s staff to the Council on Library and Information Resources and the servers and technical infrastructure to the Field Museum in Chicago. Trei, who recently ended her year-long tenure as transition director, spoke with News Bureau arts and humanities editor Jodi Heckel about the library and its future."

title: Guest Post — From Charity to Intellectual Partnership: The Global Monograph Crisis, Artificial Intelligence, and the Future of Open Access Through the Lens of Ukraine - The Scholarly Kitchen
content: "The global scholarly publishing ecosystem is experiencing a period of severe turbulence. The crisis of the university monograph is no longer a theoretical threat — it is a financial reality. Against the backdrop of a sharp decline in print academic book sales (which have plummeted by 40-50% for humanities and social sciences over the last decade in the West), a highly precarious financial runway for Open Access (OA) models, and radical pressure from Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems, academic publishing is looking for new structural anchors. Can a country currently functioning at the epicenter of a major geopolitical shift offer solutions for the global market? On May 29, 2026, within the framework of the International Book Arsenal Festival in Kyiv, a major Lab-Hub discussion titled “From Shelves and Drawers to Millions of Readers” took place. title: 10 Authors Share Why They Published Open Access - ACLS
content:
"When finalist authors of the 2026 ACLS Open Access Book Prizes explained why they published open access, several themes emerged: reaching audiences outside academia, including communities the book is about or engages with; greater accessibility for readers at under-resourced institutions; easier adoption in classrooms; and wider reach, measured in downloads and countries reached.

Their reflections also speak of a shared ethos that peer-reviewed humanities and social science research should be freely and widely available. The ACLS Open Access Book Prizes and Arcadia Open Access Publishing Awards recognize and reward this critical work through $50,000 awards to the authors and publishers of exceptional, innovative, and open access humanities books published from 2019 to 2024. Below, read the authors’ insights in their own words."

title: Strengthening and Shaping Openness in Social Sciences and Humanities – Open Research Blog Berlin
content: Abstract:  How can Open Science Communities within the Social Sciences and Humanities (SSH) be better connected to strengthen collaboration and knowledge exchange? And how can we drive Open Science (OS) forward? To answer these questions – and many more – the OPERAS  (Open scholarly communication in the European Research Area for Social Sciences and Humanities) Research Infrastructure and the SCIROS  (Strategic Collaboration for Interdisciplinary Research on Open Science in the SSH) project jointly organized a conference that took place in the impressive Staszic Palace in Warsaw, Poland. OPERAS was established to address scholarly communication needs of European SSH researchers. The SCIROS research network was launched in 2024 to strengthen OS practices within SSH.

title: Australia needs a new model of higher education built around equity | Pearls and Irritations
content: "Here, education is largely online and utilises a distributed model with central campuses largely replaced by local hubs – which can be physical or virtual. Educational resources will be open and can be shared locally and globally, increasing access to best practice resources and reducing costs all round. Research will be able to involve under-represented populations as research hubs will also be distributed rather than centralised. Publication of research will use the ‘Diamond Open Access’ model – a community-driven, academic-led, and academic-owned model allowing open access to journals and textbooks avoiding the current paywalls. The carbon footprint of higher education would be drastically reduced. The distributed model would extend to leadership, reducing managerialism, increasing academic autonomy and reducing internal inequity. Collaborative development and sharing of Open Educational Resources reduce the drive to the commodification of education, and open publishing reduces the power of commercial publishers.
